question: What if the Black Death never reached Europe?
short: Europe in 1347 was already full, hungry and stuck. The plague killed perhaps a third to a half of it, and the survivors got scarce labour, higher wages and weaker lords. Without it, the best guess is a slower, poorer, more crowded late Middle Ages, though historians split on how much the plague itself (rather than class power, climate or later epidemics) changed the path.

divergence.text: Infected rats and fleas never board the Genoese galleys that leave Caffa in 1347.

plausibility_note: Low: plague was established in Central Asian rodents and moving along Mongol-era trade routes, so a Europe that never meets it is hard to build. A delay of years or decades is easier to imagine.

steps.title: Where it came from
steps.text: Ancient DNA from 1338-39 graves near Lake Issyk-Kul in Kyrgyzstan matches the strain that later struck Europe. Plague lived in marmots and other wild rodents of the Tian Shan, so the premise of this what-if is fragile: the disease was already loose in the Mongol world.

sources.cite: Spyrou et al., The source of the Black Death in fourteenth-century central Eurasia, Nature 606 (2022)

steps.title: The jump at Caffa
steps.text: Plague broke out in the Golden Horde army besieging the Genoese port of Caffa in 1346. Gabriele de' Mussi's story of corpses hurled over the walls is famous but second-hand. By October 1347 ships had carried the disease to Constantinople and Messina.

sources.cite: Mark Wheelis, Biological warfare at the 1346 siege of Caffa, Emerging Infectious Diseases 8 (2002)

steps.title: A continent already at the ceiling
steps.text: Before the plague, Europe had roughly tripled its people since 1000 and was pressing on its land. The Great Famine of 1315-17 killed perhaps 5 to 10 percent of northern Europeans. Wages were low and rents high. This is the world the plague hit, and the world the what-if has to keep.

sources.cite: William Chester Jordan, The Great Famine (1996)

steps.title: What really happened: one in three, or worse
steps.text: Between 1347 and 1351 the plague crossed Europe from Sicily to Norway. Estimates of the dead run from about 30 percent to Ole Benedictow's 60 percent. It came back in 1361 and every decade or two for three centuries, holding population down.

sources.cite: Ole Benedictow, The Black Death 1346-1353: The Complete History (2004)

steps.title: No labour shortage, no wage boom
steps.text: In the real England, a labourer's real wage roughly doubled between the 1340s and the mid-1400s, and the crown's attempt to freeze wages (the Ordinance of Labourers, 1349) helped light the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. With the dead alive, there is no shortage to bargain with: wages stay near subsistence and the revolt, at least in that form, has no fuel.

sources.cite: Gregory Clark, The long march of history: farm wages, population and economic growth, England 1209-1869, Economic History Review 60 (2007)

steps.title: Serfdom lingers, or does it?
steps.text: After the plague, serfdom withered in the West while lords in Poland and Prussia tightened it. The same shock, opposite results. That is Robert Brenner's argument that class power, not population, decided the outcome. So in the branch the West keeps serfdom longer only if you believe the population story; on Brenner's reading the outcome is open.

sources.cite: Robert Brenner, Agrarian class structure and economic development in pre-industrial Europe, Past & Present 70 (1976)

steps.title: A slower road to the rich world
steps.text: Voigtländer and Voth argue that plague, war and crowded cities pushed Europe into a higher-income balance after 1350; Pamuk sees the plague as the start of the divergence inside Europe. In the branch, Europe stays poorer and more crowded for longer, which could weaken the high-wage push that Robert Allen sees behind Britain's labour-saving machines. Big caveat: a crowded Europe could still crash by famine, war or a later disease.

sources.cite: Nico Voigtländer and Hans-Joachim Voth, The Three Horsemen of Riches, Review of Economic Studies 80 (2013)
Şevket Pamuk, The Black Death and the origins of the Great Divergence across Europe, 1300-1600, European Review of Economic History 11 (2007)

views.name: Postan and Le Roy Ladurie
views.claim: Population drives the medieval economy; the plague reset the land-labour balance and everything followed.
views.for: Wages and rents move with population almost everywhere in Western Europe.
views.against: East and West reacted in opposite ways to the same shock.

views.name: Robert Brenner
views.claim: Who held power over peasants decided whether the shock freed them or bound them.
views.for: The second serfdom in the East.
views.against: Hard to measure class power without circular reasoning.

views.name: Bruce Campbell
views.claim: A cooling climate and pandemics together ended the medieval boom; the plague was the largest blow in a longer transition.
views.for: Tree rings and harvest records show the climate turning before 1347.
views.against: Separating climate from plague effects is hard.

unknowns: The real death toll: 30 to 60 percent depending on the scholar.
Whether plague would have arrived anyway a few years or decades later.
How much of the wage boom came from the first wave and how much from the returns of 1361 onward.

model.name: Plantagenet England
model.note: Toy Turchin-style model from the Order and Chaos lab, not fitted to England. Both runs hit a crisis in the 1340s, the toy's version of the real 1310-1400 crisis. The plague then lowers pressure on the land, so with it the next crisis comes about thirty years later than without it. Read the direction, not the dates.
